chapter_title: Adolescence — A Stage of Growth and Change
subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: What Changed? Noticing Adolescent Changes Around Us
periods.activity_description: Students anonymously write observable changes in height, voice, appearance, or strength they notice among peers onto slips, place them in a jar, and collaboratively sort the slips into categories of physical change. The class compiles a shared list of the most frequently noted changes.

roles.role_description: Facilitates the anonymous slip activity, collects and reads selected slips aloud, and guides the class in sorting observations into categories on the board.
Write one or two anonymous observations on slips, then participate in categorising the class observations into groups of physical change.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter's opening parallel — a seed growing into a seed-producing plant — and links it to human growth through infancy, childhood, adolescence, and adulthood, orienting students to the chapter's starting point.
Students write anonymous observations on slips; slips are collected and read aloud, then the class works together to group them under emerging category headings written on the board.
Teacher leads a brief discussion naming the categories: height, body structure, voice, hair, facial skin, and introduces the terms adolescence, puberty, and secondary sexual characteristics.
Students individually write one sentence defining adolescence in their own words as a quick exit check.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit grounds the chapter in students' own lived observations before any formal terminology is introduced, building from the chapter's Activity 6.1. Watch for students who conflate secondary sexual characteristics with primary reproductive organs — the chapter is careful to distinguish the two, and that distinction is worth flagging early. The exit sentence will help you judge how ready students are to move into the next unit's more precise descriptions.
materials: A jar or box for collecting slips

periods.activity_title: Mapping the Body: A Systematic Description of Adolescent Physical Changes
periods.activity_description: Students construct a structured two-column notes chart — one column for boys, one for girls — systematically recording each physical change described in the chapter: height, body structure, voice, hair, facial skin and acne. They annotate each row with the body part or mechanism involved.

roles.role_description: Guides the class through each physical change in sequence, explaining the underlying mechanism (e.g., larynx growth causing voice changes, oily secretions causing acne) before students record it.
Build the two-column chart in their notebooks, writing the change and its mechanism for each category as the teacher moves through them.

time_bands.activity: Brief recap of the previous unit's category list on the board; teacher explains that this unit adds precise mechanisms to those categories.

Teacher systematically walks through each category of physical change — height, body structure, voice and Adam's apple, body hair, acne — explaining mechanism and noting differences between boys and girls while students complete their chart.
Teacher addresses the chapter's point that variation in timing is completely normal, then asks two or three students to read a row from their chart aloud to check accuracy.
Students note one mechanism they found surprising or unfamiliar, shared briefly with a neighbour.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the categories students generated in the previous unit, now attaching precise mechanisms to each one. A common error to watch for is students describing the Adam's apple as a separate organ rather than as the visible protrusion of the growing larynx — the chapter text is explicit on this and the distinction is worth reinforcing. The completed chart will serve as a reference students can return to in later units when hormones are introduced as the underlying cause.

periods.stage_label: Classify changes as physical, reproductive, or emotional
periods.activity_title: Three Kinds of Change: Sorting Adolescent Changes by Type
periods.activity_description: Student groups receive a set of statement cards describing adolescent changes — physical, reproductive (menstrual cycle onset, reproductive maturation), and emotional (mood swings, sensitivity). Groups classify each card into one of three categories and justify their placement, then share and reconcile differences across groups.

roles.role_description: Circulates among groups, prompting justification for borderline placements and introduces the menstrual cycle and emotional changes from the chapter as groups encounter those cards.
Sort statement cards into physical, reproductive, and emotional categories, discuss disagreements within the group, and prepare one sentence of justification for each category placement.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the previous one by noting that the chart built then covered only physical changes, and poses the question: are all adolescent changes physical?
Groups work with statement cards, classifying each change and debating placements — particularly for cards about menstruation and mood swings, which may be harder to assign.

Groups share their classifications; teacher mediates disagreements, covering the chapter's content on the menstrual cycle (including its normal range and the breaking myths material) and emotional and behavioural changes from section 6.3.
Each group records a corrected final classification table in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit introduces the two new domains — reproductive and emotional change — by having students actively reason about where each change belongs, rather than receiving the classification ready-made. Watch for the common misconception that menstruation is a sign of illness; the chapter's Breaking Myths box directly addresses this, and it is worth reading the key points aloud if it arises. Groups that place mood swings under 'physical' rather than 'emotional' are making a productive error — it creates an opening to discuss how internal biological events express themselves as behaviour.
materials: Pre-written statement cards (one set per group)

periods.stage_label: Classify changes as physical, reproductive, or emotional
periods.activity_title: Emotions in Action: Mapping Feelings to Behaviours and Channels
periods.activity_description: Students individually complete a structured three-column table — emotional change, probable effect on behaviour, constructive channel — drawing on section 6.3's Activity 6.2. They then compare tables in pairs, identifying where their channels differ and discussing which channels are healthiest.

roles.role_description: Complete the three-column emotion-behaviour-channel table independently, drawing on their own experience of adolescent emotional changes as described in the chapter.
In pairs, compare completed tables, identify differences in chosen channels, and agree on two or three constructive channels to recommend.

Facilitates the pair discussion by posing probing questions and draws the class together to share recommended channels, connecting these to the chapter's examples of music, sports, and social activities.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the emotional changes category from the previous unit and explains that this unit asks students to trace what those changes do to behaviour and what to do about them.
Students complete the three-column table individually in their notebooks, identifying at least three distinct emotional changes from the chapter.
Students share tables in pairs, comparing channels chosen and discussing which are most constructive; pairs agree on their top two or three recommendations.
Brief whole-class share-out: teacher lists recommended channels on the board and connects them to the chapter's examples of music, dance, sports, and social activities.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit grounds the emotional classification from the previous unit in students' own reflective experience, using the chapter's Activity 6.2 format directly. A watch-out here is students who describe only negative emotional changes — the chapter frames heightened emotion as a normal and manageable feature of adolescence, not a deficit, and the framing of 'constructive channel' reinforces this. The pair comparison step is important: students often discover that peers channel the same emotion very differently, which sets up the next stage's focus on well-being choices.

periods.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms: hormones as the driver
periods.activity_title: The Hidden Signal: How Hormones Drive Adolescent Change
periods.activity_description: Teacher introduces hormones as chemical substances produced in different parts of the body and released on signals from the brain, explaining how they regulate growth, reproductive maturation, and mood. Students annotate a cause-and-effect diagram linking hormonal activity to the physical, reproductive, and emotional changes already classified.

roles.role_description: Explains the concept of hormones from section 6.5 — their origin, brain-signal mechanism, and the range of changes they govern — building the cause-and-effect diagram on the board step by step.

Annotate their own copy of the cause-and-effect diagram as the teacher builds it, labelling hormonal causes and linking arrows to the specific changes in each category from their earlier classification table.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the three-category classification table from the previous two units and poses the question: what single underlying cause connects all three types of change?

Teacher introduces hormones from section 6.5 — definition, production site, brain-signal mechanism — and builds a cause-and-effect diagram on the board, connecting hormonal activity to puberty, menstruation, and mood changes.
Students annotate their own diagram, adding arrows from 'hormone released' to each category of change they classified in earlier units, ensuring every change type is accounted for.
Quick verbal check: teacher asks two or three students to name one change and trace its hormonal cause using their diagram.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the conceptual pivot of the arc — students already know what changes happen and how to classify them; now they learn why. A key misconception to watch for is the idea that hormones are produced only in one location; the chapter explicitly notes they are produced in different parts of the body and released on brain signals, so the diagram should reflect multiple production sites. The annotation task is a check that students can apply the causal link to every category, not just recall the definition of hormones in isolation.

periods.stage_label: Apply causal understanding to well-being measures
periods.activity_title: Why These Choices? Linking Well-Being Measures to Adolescent Biology
periods.activity_description: Student groups are each assigned one well-being domain from section 6.4 — nutrition, hygiene, physical activity, social life, or avoiding harmful substances — and must explain why their domain is especially important during adolescence by grounding each recommendation in the biological changes studied. Groups construct a brief explanatory poster panel and present their reasoning.

roles.role_description: Analyse their assigned well-being domain from section 6.4, identify which biological changes make it necessary, and construct one poster panel with a minimum of two cause-linked recommendations.
Circulates to prompt groups to move beyond listing recommendations to explaining why each is needed biologically, and facilitates the panel presentations, drawing cross-group connections.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the previous one by explaining that knowing hormones drive adolescent change naturally raises the question: what does that mean for how adolescents should take care of themselves?

Groups work on their assigned well-being domain, using the chapter's section 6.4 content to generate at least two cause-linked explanations — e.g., why calcium matters given rapid bone growth, or why hygiene in new hair-growth areas is important given the physical changes described.
Groups present their panel in turn; class listens and may add a cause-linked reason the presenting group missed.
Teacher draws a brief summary on the board: a table with each well-being domain and its biological anchor.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit requires students to apply their causal understanding of hormonal change — built in the previous unit — to practical health reasoning, which is the chapter's applied dimension. Watch for groups that list recommendations without explanation; the key move is pushing them to answer 'why during adolescence specifically?', which forces the link back to the biology. The cyberbullying and substance abuse content in sections 6.4.4 and 6.4.5 should both be drawn into the social life and avoidance groups respectively, as these are chapter-grounded risks the chapter explicitly names.
materials: Large paper or card for poster panels

periods.stage_label: Apply causal understanding to well-being measures
periods.activity_title: Decision Points: Applying Biological and Well-Being Knowledge to New Scenarios
periods.activity_description: Students work individually through four short written scenarios, each describing an adolescent facing a choice or problem. For each scenario, they identify which biological change is involved, explain the hormonal driver, and recommend a well-being response grounded in the chapter. Written responses are shared in pairs for peer review.

roles.role_description: Respond to each scenario in writing, tracing the biological change, its hormonal cause, and the appropriate well-being measure, producing a short reasoned response for each.
In pairs, review each other's scenario responses, checking that the biological change, hormonal driver, and well-being measure are all correctly linked.
Circulates during individual work, then facilitates a whole-class review of one or two scenarios where responses diverged, making the complete chain of reasoning explicit.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the well-being domains from the previous unit and introduces the scenario task as a check on whether students can apply both biological understanding and well-being reasoning together.
Students work individually through the four scenarios in writing, each requiring a biological change identification, hormonal cause, and well-being recommendation.
Pairs exchange responses and review each other's reasoning, noting where the chain from biology to well-being measure is incomplete or incorrect.

Teacher facilitates whole-class discussion of one or two scenarios where responses diverged most, making the complete reasoning chain explicit and closing the unit by affirming the chapter's key message: understanding the biology of adolescence supports informed, healthy decision-making.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit draws together the whole arc — physical and reproductive and emotional changes, their hormonal cause, and the well-being measures that follow — by asking students to reason through realistic situations rather than simply recall information. Watch for responses that recommend a well-being measure without connecting it to any biological driver; the chapter's argument is precisely that the biology explains why the measure matters, and a recommendation without that link is incomplete. Scenarios should be drawn from the chapter's own content — a student experiencing acne, a girl managing menstrual hygiene, a student being pressured to try tobacco, or someone experiencing mood swings — so that all content is anchored in the text.
homework: Choose one well-being measure from section 6.4 and write a short explanation of how a specific biological change during adolescence makes that measure necessary, using the cause-effect reasoning practised in this unit.

Read the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan box in section 6.4.5 and explain in two or three sentences why adolescence is described as a particularly vulnerable time for substance abuse, connecting your answer to the hormonal and emotional changes covered in the chapter.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe, name, and systematically describe the physical changes of adolescence — height, body structure, voice, hair, facial skin and acne — recording mechanisms in a structured chart.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can name and describe the observable physical changes of adolescence, state the body mechanism involved in each (e.g., larynx growth, oily secretions), and distinguish secondary sexual characteristics from primary reproductive changes.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify changes as physical, reproductive, or emotional
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify a full set of adolescent changes — including menstrual cycle onset, mood swings, and secondary sexual characteristics — into physical, reproductive, and emotional categories, justifying each placement and mapping emotions to constructive behavioural channels.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can correctly classify adolescent changes as physical, reproductive, or emotional, provide a justification for borderline cases (e.g., menstruation, mood swings), and identify constructive behavioural channels for emotional changes.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms: hormones as the driver
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students learn that hormones — chemical substances produced in different body parts and released on brain signals — are the underlying biological cause of all three categories of adolescent change, and annotate a cause-and-effect diagram linking hormonal activity to specific changes.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can explain what hormones are, describe how the brain-signal-production-release mechanism works, and trace the hormonal cause for at least one change in each of the three categories (physical, reproductive, emotional).

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Apply causal understanding to well-being measures
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students apply their biological and hormonal understanding to explain why specific well-being measures — nutrition, hygiene, physical activity, balanced social life, avoiding harmful substances — are especially necessary during adolescence, and reason through scenarios linking biological change to well-being response.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can identify and explain measures for maintaining overall well-being during adolescence, grounding each measure in the specific biological or hormonal change that makes it necessary, and apply this reasoning to novel scenarios.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can name and describe the observable physical changes of adolescence, state the body mechanism involved in each (e.g., larynx growth, oily secretions), and distinguish secondary sexual characteristics from primary reproductive changes.

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: During adolescence, boys often develop a hoarse or cracking voice. What is the body mechanism that directly causes this change?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased production of oily secretions from skin pores causes the vocal cords to thicken.

options.label: B
options.text: Growth of the larynx (voice box) makes the voice deeper and sometimes hoarse.

options.label: C
options.text: The Adam's apple is a separate organ that grows independently and stretches the vocal cords.

options.label: D
options.text: Rapid increase in height causes the windpipe to lengthen, lowering the pitch of the voice.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses two separate mechanisms — oily secretions (cause of acne) and voice change — indicating the student has not distinguished the mechanisms for different physical changes.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Treats the Adam's apple as an independent organ rather than as the visible external protrusion of the growing larynx, a specific misconception the chapter text directly corrects.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Applies a plausible-sounding physical analogy (height increase lengthening the windpipe) that has no basis in the chapter, indicating recall of height change without understanding of the voice mechanism.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with written options can be asked verbally to point to the part of the body responsible for voice and describe what happens to it. Alternatively, a simple diagram of the throat with labelled larynx and Adam's apple can be provided as a visual anchor.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can name and describe the observable physical changes of adolescence, state the body mechanism involved in each (e.g., larynx growth, oily secretions), and distinguish secondary sexual characteristics from primary reproductive changes.

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: Which of the following correctly describes what secondary sexual characteristics are?

options.label: A
options.text: Changes that directly produce eggs or sperm and are essential for reproduction.

options.label: B
options.text: Changes such as the appearance of body hair and voice deepening that help distinguish males from females but are not directly involved in reproduction.

options.label: C
options.text: Changes that occur only in girls, such as breast development and onset of the menstrual cycle.

options.label: D
options.text: Changes that occur only during the final years of adolescence when the body is fully adult.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses secondary sexual characteristics with primary reproductive functions — the exact distinction the chapter draws — indicating the student has not grasped the defining feature of 'secondary'.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Restricts secondary sexual characteristics to girls only, ignoring the chapter's clear statement that both boys and girls display them (body hair, voice) and misclassifying menstruation as secondary rather than reproductive.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Applies a timing-based definition not present in the chapter, suggesting the student is reasoning by association with 'late' rather than by the chapter's functional definition.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can demonstrate the same understanding by giving two concrete examples — one from boys, one from girls — and explaining in a sentence why each does not directly cause reproduction. This verbal or written alternative sidesteps the need to recall the formal term.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can correctly classify adolescent changes as physical, reproductive, or emotional, provide a justification for borderline cases (e.g., menstruation, mood swings), and identify constructive behavioural channels for emotional changes.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Change | Category chosen by student
Onset of menstrual cycle | ?

assessment_items.question_text: A student is classifying adolescent changes into physical, reproductive, or emotional categories. Refer to the table provided. Which row shows an incorrect classification?

options.label: A
options.text: Onset of menstrual cycle → Physical

options.label: B
options.text: Mood swings and heightened sensitivity → Emotional

options.label: C
options.text: Growth of facial hair in boys → Physical

options.label: D
options.text: Increase in height and weight → Physical

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student incorrectly flags a correct classification, suggesting they may be uncertain whether emotional changes belong to a separate category or are a subtype of physical change.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student incorrectly flags a correct classification, possibly because facial hair is associated with reproduction in common thinking rather than being understood as a secondary sexual characteristic classified as physical.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student incorrectly flags a correct classification, which may indicate confusion about the category system itself rather than a specific misconception about height and weight.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to identify the incorrect row can be asked to write a justification for the menstrual cycle's category — explaining what function it relates to — which surfaces the reasoning needed without the comparison task.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify changes as physical, reproductive, or emotional
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can correctly classify adolescent changes as physical, reproductive, or emotional, provide a justification for borderline cases (e.g., menstruation, mood swings), and identify constructive behavioural channels for emotional changes.

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: An adolescent feels unusually anxious before a sports event and finds it hard to concentrate. According to the chapter's framework, which response best channels this emotional change constructively?

options.label: A
options.text: Recognise the anxiety as a normal emotional change and channel it into physical activity or focused preparation for the event.

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the anxiety as a sign of poor physical health and consult a doctor for nutritional deficiencies.

options.label: C
options.text: Avoid the event to prevent the emotional discomfort from affecting performance.

options.label: D
options.text: Classify the anxiety as a reproductive change and recognise it as a normal part of puberty's internal changes.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Misclassifies an emotional change as a physical or nutritional problem, collapsing the chapter's three-category distinction and missing the emotional domain entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Represents avoidance rather than constructive channelling — the student may understand the classification but not the chapter's guidance on channelling emotions through activity.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misclassifies emotional change as reproductive, a category confusion the chapter's three-part framework is designed to prevent.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can respond verbally by naming the category of change, then suggesting one channel from their own experience or the chapter's examples — music, dance, sports, or social activities — without needing to select from written options.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify changes as physical, reproductive, or emotional
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can correctly classify adolescent changes as physical, reproductive, or emotional, provide a justification for borderline cases (e.g., menstruation, mood swings), and identify constructive behavioural channels for emotional changes.

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: A classmate tells you that menstruation is a sign of illness and that girls who are menstruating should avoid physical activity. Using what you have learned, explain why this statement is incorrect and classify menstruation correctly within the changes of adolescence.
expected_elements: Identifies menstruation as a reproductive change (not a sign of illness) and places it in the reproductive category of adolescent changes.
States that menstruation is a normal, recurring cycle associated with reproductive maturity, typically beginning at puberty.
Rejects the restriction on physical activity as having no scientific basis, as supported by the chapter's Breaking Myths material.
Notes that the menstrual cycle has a normal duration and range (21–35 days cycle; 3–7 days of menstruation) as evidence that it is a predictable biological process, not a pathological one.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write a full explanation can respond by first simply classifying menstruation (reproductive, not illness), then adding one reason for their classification. Oral responses to the same question are equally valid as a demonstration of the classification and justification.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms: hormones as the driver
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can explain what hormones are, describe how the brain-signal-production-release mechanism works, and trace the hormonal cause for at least one change in each of the three categories (physical, reproductive, emotional).

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: Which statement best describes how hormones cause changes during adolescence?

options.label: A
options.text: Hormones are produced only in the brain, which directly controls all physical and emotional changes during adolescence.

options.label: B
options.text: Hormones are chemical substances produced in different parts of the body in response to signals from the brain, and they regulate growth, development, reproduction, and behaviour.

options.label: C
options.text: Hormones are nutrients absorbed from food that trigger puberty when enough have accumulated in the body.

options.label: D
options.text: Hormones are produced only during emotional events, which is why mood swings are more common than physical changes during adolescence.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Locates hormone production exclusively in the brain, confusing the site of signal origin with the sites of hormone production — a specific error the chapter's multi-site description is designed to prevent.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates hormones with nutrients, possibly drawing on the chapter's nearby nutrition content; indicates the student has not grasped the chapter's distinction between chemical messengers and dietary substances.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Restricts hormonal activity to emotional triggers only, ignoring the chapter's explicit statement that hormones regulate physical growth and reproduction as well.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can demonstrate the same understanding by drawing a simple flow diagram: brain signal → hormone produced in body part → change (physical / reproductive / emotional). This visual production task is an alternative demonstration pathway.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms: hormones as the driver
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can explain what hormones are, describe how the brain-signal-production-release mechanism works, and trace the hormonal cause for at least one change in each of the three categories (physical, reproductive, emotional).

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'Hormones only cause puberty and menstruation — mood swings during adolescence have a completely different cause.' Using the chapter's explanation of hormones, identify the flaw in this reasoning.

options.label: A
options.text: The student is correct: mood swings are caused by social pressures during adolescence, not by hormonal activity.

options.label: B
options.text: The student is incorrect: the chapter states that mood changes during adolescence are also primarily driven by hormonal activity, making all three types of change — physical, reproductive, and emotional — hormonally linked.

options.label: C
options.text: The student is partially correct: hormones cause puberty but menstruation has a separate nutritional cause related to iron deficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: The student is incorrect only because mood swings are caused by growth of the brain, which is a physical change, not an emotional one.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Accepts the student's flawed claim at face value, attributing mood swings to social causes only — indicating the student has not connected the chapter's hormonal explanation to the emotional category.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Separates menstruation from hormonal causation and attributes it to nutrition, conflating the chapter's iron deficiency health content with the chapter's causal explanation of menstruation — a confusion between two distinct content sections.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Attempts to rescue the connection by reclassifying mood swings as physical changes, which avoids the core issue: the chapter explicitly states mood changes are hormonally driven, regardless of category.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can respond by locating the specific sentence in the chapter (section 6.5) that links mood changes to hormonal activity and reading it aloud or copying it, then explaining in one sentence why this contradicts the student's claim.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms: hormones as the driver
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can explain what hormones are, describe how the brain-signal-production-release mechanism works, and trace the hormonal cause for at least one change in each of the three categories (physical, reproductive, emotional).

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: Using the chapter's explanation of hormones, trace the cause-and-effect chain for two of the following changes: (a) onset of puberty and voice change in boys; (b) onset of the menstrual cycle; (c) mood swings during adolescence. For each change you choose, state the hormonal cause and name the category of change it belongs to.
expected_elements: Defines hormones as chemical substances produced in different parts of the body in response to signals from the brain.
For each chosen change: names the category (physical, reproductive, or emotional) correctly.
For each chosen change: states that the change is driven by hormonal activity as described in section 6.5.
The chain is complete: brain signal → hormone released → specific change named.
Uses at least one correctly named body mechanism (e.g., larynx growth for voice change) alongside the hormonal cause.

SCR.inclusivity: Students can complete this task as a labelled flow diagram rather than prose, as long as the three elements — brain signal, hormone, specific change — are present and linked. Students who can articulate only one full chain clearly should receive credit for that chain while being prompted to attempt the second.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply causal understanding to well-being measures
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify and explain measures for maintaining overall well-being during adolescence, grounding each measure in the specific biological or hormonal change that makes it necessary, and apply this reasoning to novel scenarios.

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: An adolescent's diet lacks calcium-rich foods such as milk, millets, and curd. Which consequence does the chapter predict, and why is this consequence specifically a concern during adolescence?

options.label: A
options.text: The adolescent will develop acne, because calcium deficiency increases oily secretions from skin pores.

options.label: B
options.text: The adolescent will have reduced bone growth, because adolescence is a period of rapid physical change that places especially high demand on calcium for optimal bone development.

options.label: C
options.text: The adolescent will experience more mood swings, because calcium is the nutrient that regulates hormonal balance during puberty.

options.label: D
options.text: The adolescent will develop iron-deficiency anaemia, because milk is the primary source of iron during adolescence.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the nutritional role of calcium with the skin mechanism of acne — conflating two different content sections (6.4.1 and 6.1) without a causal link between them.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents a causal link between calcium and hormonal mood regulation that has no basis in the chapter, likely by combining nearby content on hormones and mood with the nutrition section without a grounded connection.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses calcium deficiency with iron deficiency anaemia — two distinct nutritional concerns the chapter covers separately — and misidentifies milk as the primary iron source when the chapter lists spinach, kidney beans, and dried fruits for iron.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be asked to identify which section of the chapter covers bone growth and calcium, read the relevant sentence, and then explain in their own words why adolescence makes this especially important — a scaffolded version of the same reasoning task.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply causal understanding to well-being measures
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify and explain measures for maintaining overall well-being during adolescence, grounding each measure in the specific biological or hormonal change that makes it necessary, and apply this reasoning to novel scenarios.

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: A friend offers an adolescent a cigarette, saying 'Just try it once — it won't make you addicted.' Using the chapter's explanation of substance abuse during adolescence, identify the flaw in this reasoning.

options.label: A
options.text: The flaw is that cigarettes only affect lung capacity and not any other health dimension, so the risk is limited.

options.label: B
options.text: The flaw is that addictive substances create a compulsive urge to continue once consumed, so 'just once' can be the start of substance abuse, which is especially risky during the vulnerable period of adolescence.

options.label: C
options.text: The flaw is that cigarettes are only dangerous when combined with other substances like alcohol, so a single cigarette is genuinely harmless.

options.label: D
options.text: The flaw is that the friend is motivated by cyberbullying, which the chapter identifies as the main cause of substance abuse in adolescents.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Understates the health consequences by reducing them to lung capacity only, missing the chapter's broader list of effects — breathing difficulties, memory loss — and missing the addictive mechanism entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents a combination-harm condition not present in the chapter, suggesting the student is reasoning by analogy rather than from the chapter's actual addictive-substance explanation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Conflates two separate chapter topics — cyberbullying (6.4.4) and substance abuse (6.4.5) — treating them as causally linked when the chapter presents them as distinct risks.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can respond by reading the definition of addiction and substance abuse from section 6.4.5 and then restating in their own words why 'just once' is the precise moment the risk begins — a close-reading task that produces the same reasoning.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply causal understanding to well-being measures
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify and explain measures for maintaining overall well-being during adolescence, grounding each measure in the specific biological or hormonal change that makes it necessary, and apply this reasoning to novel scenarios.

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: A health organisation is designing a well-being programme for adolescents. They plan to include only two measures: (i) nutritional guidance and (ii) advice on avoiding harmful substances. A student argues that personal hygiene and physical activity should also be included. Using the biological changes of adolescence to support the argument, evaluate whether the student's suggestion is justified and explain what would be lost from the programme without these two additional measures.
look_for: Connects the need for personal hygiene specifically to the new physical changes of adolescence — body hair growth in armpits and pubic region, and menstruation — rather than offering hygiene as a general life advice.
Connects physical activity to both physical well-being (stamina, health during rapid growth) and emotional/mental well-being (mood improvement) as described in section 6.4.3.
Evaluates the programme gap: identifies at least one specific biological change that would be insufficiently addressed without each of the two proposed additions.
Reaches a reasoned conclusion that the student's suggestion is justified, with the reasoning grounded in the chapter's biological change content rather than general health knowledge.
Demonstrates the ability to weigh two competing positions (the organisation's plan vs. the student's argument) rather than simply listing all well-being measures.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to construct the evaluation argument can begin by producing a table: biological change in one column, well-being measure it requires in the second. Once the table is complete, they use it to answer whether the programme is complete. This scaffolded entry point produces equivalent evidence of the same reasoning.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify and explain measures for maintaining overall well-being during adolescence, grounding each measure in the specific biological or hormonal change that makes it necessary, and apply this reasoning to novel scenarios.

competency.competency_text: Describing biological and hormonal changes that occur during adolescence and identifying measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Biological change involved | Hormonal driver? (Yes/No + brief reason) | Well-being measure needed | Why this measure specifically during adolescence
Devyani, 13, has been skipping meals saying she doesn't feel hungry. Her friends notice she is tired and pale. | | | | 
Venkatesh, 12, is being pressured by older boys to try gutka. He feels embarrassed to say no. | | | 
Aria, 14, feels intense anxiety before exams and has been spending all her time alone in her room. | | | |

assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. Four adolescents are facing different situations. For each scenario: (1) identify the biological change involved, (2) state whether hormonal activity is a driver and give a brief reason, (3) name the well-being measure most needed, and (4) explain why that measure is specifically important during adolescence rather than at any other life stage.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use what you have learned about the biological and hormonal changes of adolescence and the well-being measures in sections 6.4 and 6.5 to complete the table. For each row, trace the chain from biological change → hormonal link → well-being need → reason it matters now.
format_of_output: Completed table with all four columns filled for each scenario
At least one row where the 'Why specifically during adolescence' column references a named biological change rather than general health advice

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Data interpretation task (provided table or graph)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The table format directly mirrors the scenario-based reasoning practised in the final two units of the lesson plan, requiring students to trace a chain from biological change to hormonal driver to well-being measure across four distinct adolescent situations — the most natural demonstration vehicle for the stage's convergent implied LO.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response evidences the student's ability to integrate all four elements of the chapter's arc — identifying biological changes, tracing their hormonal cause, selecting appropriate well-being measures, and justifying why each measure is especially necessary during adolescence specifically — across varied, novel scenarios.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students to use sections 6.4 and 6.5 together, signalling that neither biological knowledge nor well-being knowledge alone is sufficient — the chain must be complete. The column structure ensures every element is made explicit rather than implied.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses name a specific biological change for each scenario (e.g., rapid bone growth for Devyani, secondary sexual characteristics and oily secretions for Rohan), state a hormonal link with a brief reason, and justify the well-being measure by connecting it to that specific change rather than to general health. Weak responses list well-being measures correctly but do not connect them to a biological change, or use generic justifications ('because it is healthy') that could apply at any life stage.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the full table challenging can complete two of the four rows fully before attempting the others, or can respond to each scenario verbally with the teacher recording key points. Students who struggle to name the biological change can be directed to their class notes or the relevant chapter section before completing the table.
